chapter_summary: Proverbs 26 is a concentrated study in foolishness, laziness, and deceit. The chapter opens with a series of vivid images showing that honour given to a fool is disordered and even dangerous. It then exposes the laziness of the sluggard, who makes wild excuses and never rises to meet life. The final section confronts the subtle sins of the tongue — gossip, flattery, and covered hatred — warning that wickedness disguised with smooth words will ultimately be exposed. Throughout, God is shown as the one who forms all things and who cannot be permanently deceived.
main_lesson: A fool keeps going back to the same wrong choices. But God sees everything — even hidden wickedness will one day be brought into the light.

memory_verse.kjv: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
memory_verse.little_bible: A dog goes back to its vomit. A fool keeps going back to doing wrong.

parent_guide:
Proverbs 26 opens with a concentration of 'fool' sayings that can feel repetitive until you notice the cumulative point: foolishness is not simply ignorance — it is a pattern. A fool is defined by going back to the same errors (v. 11), by refusing correction (vv. 3–5), and by trusting their own judgment above all others (v. 12). For children, this section of Proverbs is a mirror: it asks whether they are learning from correction or cycling back to the same disobedience. The standard remedy is not more information but humility and the willingness to change.

The laziness section (vv. 13–16) is among the most satirical in Proverbs. The sluggard invents a lion in the street to avoid going out. He turns on his bed like a door on its hinges — motion without progress. He is too tired even to bring food to his mouth, yet he considers himself wiser than seven thoughtful men. The portrait is deliberately comic, but the warning is serious: laziness hides behind excuses, and it quietly destroys a life. Help your children see that excuses, delay, and 'I'll do it later' are early signs of the sluggard's spirit.

The final section (vv. 17–28) turns to the destructive power of the tongue. Gossip is likened to wounds that sink deep (v. 22). Flattery — smooth words that hide a wicked heart — is compared to shining silver covering a filthy piece of broken pottery (v. 23). The chapter ends with a thunderous truth: you cannot cover wickedness forever. The pit-digger falls in; the stone-roller is crushed by it (v. 27). A lying tongue and a flattering mouth ultimately destroy the very people they deceive (v. 28).

For family discipleship, this chapter is a rich warning against three sins children will encounter early and often: foolish patterns, lazy habits, and dishonest words. Challenge your children: When I correct you, are you learning or just waiting to do it again? Are you finding excuses not to do what you know you should? Are your words honest, or are you trying to sound nice while hiding what you really think or feel?
application_for_children: This week, when you feel like going back to something you know is wrong — stop and choose differently. Ask God to help you change. And always speak the truth, even when it is hard.

verses.kjv: As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool.
verses.little_bible: Snow in summer does not belong. Rain at harvest does not fit. Giving honour to a fool does not fit either.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Just like snow in summer, honour does not fit a fool.
verses.meaning: Snow in summer and rain at harvest are not just unusual — they are harmful. Snow ruins summer crops; rain at harvest ruins the grain. In the same way, giving honour to a fool is not merely inappropriate, it is damaging to the community. Honour must be earned by wisdom and righteousness, not merely assigned.
verses.prayer: God, help me to be wise and worthy of honour.
verses.discussion_question: Why does honour only belong to someone who is wise?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach children to give honour to the right people — those who are wise, faithful, and godly — rather than to those who are simply popular or loud?
verses.do_it_today: Think of someone wise and good in your life. Tell them you respect them today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child looking confused as snow falls on a summer garden full of bright flowers, a warm bright sun and cold snow together, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come.
verses.little_bible: A bird flies and wanders freely. But a curse without a real reason will not land. Undeserved curses cannot stick.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A curse with no reason flies away like a bird.
verses.meaning: As a sparrow or swallow darts through the air and lands nowhere permanently, so a curse that has no just cause will not take hold. God governs the moral order; accusations and curses aimed at the innocent are not automatically effective. This is a comfort to those falsely accused and a warning to those who curse carelessly.
verses.prayer: God, protect me from unfair harm.
verses.discussion_question: What happens to a curse that is not deserved?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children trust God's protection when someone speaks falsely against them — not to take revenge, but to trust God's moral order?
verses.do_it_today: If someone said something mean or unfair about you lately, tell God. Trust Him to guard you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A small sparrow darting freely through bright open sky, curving and soaring, no place to land, soft clouds, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back.
verses.little_bible: A horse needs a whip to keep moving. A donkey needs a bridle to be guided. A fool needs correction to change.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Animals need guidance. Fools need firm correction too.
verses.meaning: This is a practical and unsentimental observation: animals respond to the right form of control, and so does the fool. The fool is not managed by gentle suggestion alone — strong, clear correction is necessary. This does not celebrate cruelty but reflects the reality that wisdom sometimes requires firm discipline.
verses.prayer: God, help me accept correction and learn.
verses.discussion_question: Why do some things only change with firm correction?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that the loving application of discipline is not harshness but care — the same way a bridle steers a donkey safely?
verses.do_it_today: When a parent corrects you today, say 'thank you' and mean it. Correction is a gift.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child looking at a horse wearing a bridle being gently guided, the horse calm and directed, warm rural setting, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.
verses.little_bible: Do not argue back in a foolish way. If you do, you become foolish too.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Do not argue back like a fool. You might act like one.
verses.meaning: When a fool speaks nonsense, replying in kind — matching their tone, their logic, or their anger — drags you down to their level. The wise person recognises that some conversations will pull you into foolishness if you engage carelessly. Restraint is wisdom.
verses.prayer: God, help me stay wise when others do not.
verses.discussion_question: What happens when you argue like a fool?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach children to disengage from foolish arguments without being rude — developing the wisdom to know when engagement will only make things worse?
verses.do_it_today: If someone says something silly or mean today, try walking away calmly instead of arguing back.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child turning calmly and walking away from another child yelling, peace on the calm child's face, warm playground scene, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.
verses.little_bible: Sometimes you must correct a fool. If you stay silent, he will think he is wise when he is not.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Sometimes a fool needs to be corrected so he knows he is wrong.
verses.meaning: Placed immediately after verse 4, this creates a deliberate tension: sometimes you should not engage, and sometimes you must. The difference lies in the outcome. When silence will allow the fool to grow more proud and dangerous in their error, a wise and truthful response is necessary. This pair of verses teaches situational discernment.
verses.prayer: God, give me wisdom to know when to speak.
verses.discussion_question: When is it right to correct someone who is being foolish?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children develop the discernment to know when speaking up is necessary (to prevent greater harm) versus when silence is the wiser path?
verses.do_it_today: Ask a parent: 'When should I speak up and when should I walk away?' Listen carefully to their answer.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child thoughtfully raising a hand to gently correct another child who looks confused, kind expression, warm classroom scene, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage.
verses.little_bible: Sending a fool with an important message is a big mistake. It is like cutting off your own feet. You will get hurt.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Trusting a fool with an important job will cause harm.
verses.meaning: Sending a fool with a crucial message is self-defeating — the message will be garbled, delayed, or turned to harm. 'Cutting off the feet' pictures removing one's own ability to act effectively. To trust a fool with important tasks is to guarantee failure and damage.
verses.memory_phrase: Trust wise people with important things.
verses.prayer: God, help me to be trustworthy and reliable.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it important to choose the right person for an important job?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that earning trust and responsibility comes through demonstrated reliability in small things first?
verses.do_it_today: Do one small task today without being asked. Show that you can be trusted.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child holding a sealed letter, looking uncertain, passing it to someone careless who is distracted, warm tones, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The legs of the lame are not equal: so is a parable in the mouth of fools.
verses.little_bible: A lame person's legs do not work right. Wise words in a fool's mouth do not work right either.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool cannot use wise words any better than a lame person can run.
verses.meaning: A fool cannot effectively use a wise saying any more than a lame man can use unequal legs to walk straight. Wisdom is not just having the right words — it is having the character, understanding, and life that makes those words ring true. A fool misuses and misapplies wisdom.
verses.prayer: God, give me a wise heart, not just wise words.
verses.discussion_question: Can someone say wise words but still act foolishly?
verses.family_discussion: How do we raise children who internalise wisdom rather than merely recite it — whose lives match their words?
verses.do_it_today: Think of a wise thing you know is true. Ask yourself: 'Do I actually live this way?'
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with a scroll of wise words but looking confused about what they mean, gentle puzzled expression, warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: As he that bindeth a stone in a sling, so is he that giveth honour to a fool.
verses.little_bible: Tying a stone in a sling so it cannot fly is useless. Giving honour to a fool is just as useless.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Giving honour to a fool is as pointless as a tied-up sling.
verses.meaning: A sling with its stone tied in is worthless — it defeats the very purpose of the tool. Similarly, honour poured on a fool is wasted and self-defeating. Honour is a tool that only functions properly when directed at those who merit it. Misplaced honour corrupts communities.
verses.prayer: God, help me honour the right people.
verses.discussion_question: What goes wrong when we honour the wrong person?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children develop a culture of giving honour to those who genuinely model wisdom and godliness — rather than to whoever is most entertaining or popular?
verses.do_it_today: Tell a wise, kind person in your life why you look up to them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child holding a sling with a stone firmly tied in — useless, frustrated expression, gentle humour in the scene, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: As a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouths of fools.
verses.little_bible: A drunk man grabs a thorn branch and hurts himself without knowing it. A fool uses wise words and hurts others the same way.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool using wise words can accidentally hurt, like a thorn in a drunk man's hand.
verses.meaning: A drunkard who grabs a thorny branch is a danger to himself and others — he cannot feel or control what he is wielding. So the fool who wields proverbs and wisdom sayings without understanding causes damage without even recognising it. Wisdom misused is a weapon.
verses.prayer: God, help me understand Your words before I share them.
verses.discussion_question: How can someone cause harm with words they do not really understand?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children understand that quoting Scripture or wisdom without understanding it can be misleading and even harmful — and that depth matters more than volume?
verses.do_it_today: Before you share something you have heard or read, ask a parent if you have understood it correctly.
verses.illustration_prompt: A confused child waving a stick with thorns without realising others are getting hurt nearby, warm worried scene, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The great God that formed all things both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors.
verses.little_bible: The great God made everything. He will give to the fool what the fool deserves. He will give to those who do wrong what they deserve.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: God made all things. He will reward everyone according to what they have done.
verses.meaning: God is not absent from the moral disorder described in this chapter. He is the Creator of all things and the One who ultimately brings recompense. Both the fool and the transgressor will receive what is due to them. This is a reminder that God's justice operates even when human communities fail to enforce it.
verses.prayer: God, help me fear You and do right always.
verses.discussion_question: What does it mean that God rewards everyone according to their choices?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop a reverence for divine justice — understanding that God's ultimate accounting means no wrong goes unaddressed and no faithfulness goes unrewarded?
verses.do_it_today: Think about one of your choices today. Ask: 'Is this the kind of choice I want God to see and reward?'
verses.illustration_prompt: A large glowing balance scale held in heavenly light, one side showing foolish choices and the other faithful ones, warm golden watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
verses.little_bible: A dog goes back to its vomit. It is disgusting. A fool keeps going back to the same wrong things.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool goes back to wrong choices again and again, like a dog going back to its vomit.
verses.meaning: The image is deliberately revolting. A dog returning to its vomit is senseless and repulsive — yet the fool's return to folly is exactly as senseless and just as spiritually repulsive to God. Foolishness is not a single bad choice; it is the pattern of returning to what has already proven harmful. The New Testament quotes this verse (2 Peter 2:22) in describing those who return to sin after hearing the truth.
verses.memory_phrase: Do not go back to wrong.
verses.prayer: God, help me not go back to wrong things.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it foolish to keep doing something you know is wrong?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children identify patterns of returning to the same disobedience — and invite the Holy Spirit's power to actually change rather than simply feel sorry again?
verses.do_it_today: Is there a wrong thing you keep going back to? Tell God about it right now and ask for His help to really stop.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child looking at a path they have already been down before, footprints going back to the same wrong place, regret on their face, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
verses.little_bible: A man who thinks he is always right is in great danger. There is more hope for a fool than for him.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A person who thinks they are always right is harder to help than even a fool.
verses.meaning: Pride is more dangerous than foolishness because it closes the door to correction. A fool might be corrected; a person who is 'wise in their own conceit' will not accept correction at all. Self-righteousness and arrogance make a person unteachable — and that is the most spiritually perilous state.
verses.prayer: God, keep me humble. Help me always learn.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it dangerous to think you are never wrong?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate intellectual humility in our children — the ability to say 'I was wrong' or 'I don't know' — without undermining their confidence?
verses.do_it_today: Find one thing you were wrong about this week. Tell a parent or friend 'I was wrong about that.' Practice it.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with arms crossed and a smug expression turning away from a teacher trying to help, warm scene that shows the child missing out, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The slothful man saith, There is a lion in the way; a lion is in the streets.
verses.little_bible: The lazy man makes up excuses. He says a lion is blocking the road. He will not go out at all.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A lazy person always finds an excuse not to do the work.
verses.meaning: The sluggard's excuse is absurd — a lion in the streets was vanishingly rare. Proverbs uses this to satirise how laziness inflates tiny obstacles into impossibilities. The lazy person always has a reason why today is not the day to begin. This is a pattern of avoidance dressed as caution.
verses.prayer: God, help me not to make excuses.
verses.discussion_question: What excuses do you sometimes use to avoid doing what is right?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children notice when they are making excuses — and develop the courage and honesty to simply say 'I didn't feel like it' rather than fabricating reasons?
verses.do_it_today: Find one task you have been putting off with an excuse. Do it right now.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child sitting in bed pointing dramatically outside at an empty street, imagining a lion that is not really there, warm humorous watercolour scene

verses.kjv: As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
verses.little_bible: A door turns on its hinges but goes nowhere. A lazy person turns over in bed the same way. Lots of movement, no progress.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A lazy person turns in bed like a door on its hinges — moving but going nowhere.
verses.meaning: The image is perfectly chosen: a door swings back and forth on its hinges but goes nowhere and accomplishes nothing. The sluggard's restless turning in bed is identical — motion without progress, activity without purpose. Laziness is not always stillness; sometimes it is purposeless movement.
verses.prayer: God, help me get up and do what is good.
verses.discussion_question: What is the difference between moving and making progress?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop a sense of purposeful action — understanding that being busy is not the same as being productive or faithful?
verses.do_it_today: Get up earlier than usual tomorrow. Do one helpful thing before breakfast.
verses.illustration_prompt: A door swinging back and forth on hinges compared with a child turning over in bed, side-by-side warm watercolour scene with gentle humour

verses.kjv: The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth.
verses.little_bible: The lazy man hides his hand and will not even lift it to eat. He is too lazy to feed himself.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: The lazy person is too tired to even lift their hand to eat.
verses.meaning: This is the satirical height of the laziness portrait — the sluggard is so averse to effort that even eating, the most basic act of self-care, is too much trouble. Proverbs uses comic exaggeration to drive home the absurdity and danger of a life governed by avoiding effort.
verses.prayer: God, help me work hard at everything I do.
verses.discussion_question: What happens when laziness takes over every part of life?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children develop a work ethic that is rooted not in fear of failure but in love for God and care for others — working as unto the Lord?
verses.do_it_today: Do one chore at home today without being asked. Give your best effort.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child slumped in a chair at a dinner table with food right in front of them, hand barely raised, gentle comic expression, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
verses.little_bible: The lazy man thinks he is smarter than seven wise men. He is too proud to listen to anyone.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: The lazy person thinks they know more than all the wise people around them.
verses.meaning: This verse combines the themes of laziness and pride. The sluggard not only avoids work but refuses correction because he is convinced of his own superior wisdom. Pride and laziness feed each other: the lazy person justifies inaction with imagined cleverness. Seven wise men cannot reach someone who has already decided they know best.
verses.prayer: God, keep me humble and hard-working.
verses.discussion_question: How does pride make laziness even more dangerous?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children notice the combination of laziness and pride in themselves — the tendency to avoid hard work and then justify it by claiming they already know better?
verses.do_it_today: Ask someone today: 'What could I do better?' Listen without defending yourself.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child leaning back smugly while seven others around them are thoughtfully working and studying, warm classroom scene, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
verses.little_bible: Grabbing a strange dog by the ears is dangerous. Jumping into a fight that is not yours is just as dangerous.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Jumping into someone else's fight is like grabbing a dog by the ears — you will get hurt.
verses.meaning: Grabbing a dog by the ears — especially a strange dog — is foolish and provocative. The dog will turn and bite. So the person who inserts themselves into others' quarrels without invitation will find the conflict turning on them. Wisdom knows which battles to enter and which to pass by.
verses.prayer: God, help me know when to step back.
verses.discussion_question: When is it wise to stay out of an argument?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop the discernment to distinguish between a conflict that needs their voice (injustice, someone being hurt) and one that they should simply avoid?
verses.do_it_today: If you see two friends argue today, pray for them instead of joining in.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child reaching out to grab a dog's ears, the dog turning to snap, surprise on the child's face, gentle warning scene, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death,
verses.little_bible: Imagine a madman throwing fire, shooting arrows, and causing death all around him.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A madman throws fire and causes harm all around him.
verses.meaning: This verse begins a two-part comparison (completed in verse 19). The picture of a madman hurling firebrands, arrows, and deadly weapons describes someone utterly reckless and destructive. The power of the image lies in its completeness: fire, arrows, and death cover destruction at every distance.
verses.prayer: God, help me not harm others with my words or actions.
verses.discussion_question: How does reckless behaviour hurt the people around you?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that 'I was just playing' or 'I was just joking' does not undo real harm caused by careless actions or words?
verses.do_it_today: Think before you act today. Ask: 'Could this hurt someone?'
verses.illustration_prompt: A wild figure throwing flaming torches carelessly in all directions, chaos and sparks everywhere, a warning scene in warm watercolour tones

verses.kjv: So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
verses.little_bible: That is what the man is like who lies to his neighbour and then says, 'I was only joking!' He is just as dangerous.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Saying 'I was just joking' after hurting someone with lies is not an excuse.
verses.meaning: The punchline of the two-verse comparison: the man who deceives his neighbour and then dismisses it as 'just a joke' is as dangerous as the madman in verse 18. The casualness of the deceit — the 'Am not I in sport?' — makes it worse, not better. Claiming it was fun does not undo the fire and arrows of dishonesty.
verses.prayer: God, help me never hurt others with lies.
verses.discussion_question: Why is 'I was just joking' not a good excuse for lying?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children understand that intent does not erase impact — that harm caused 'in fun' is still harm, and must be owned rather than excused?
verses.do_it_today: If you have ever lied and said 'just joking,' think of one person to apologise to today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child laughing and saying 'just joking!' while another child stands hurt and upset nearby, the contrast between the two expressions, warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
verses.little_bible: A fire without wood will go out. Fights and quarrels without a gossip will also stop.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: No wood means no fire. No gossip means no fighting.
verses.meaning: Gossip is the fuel of conflict. Remove it, and disputes die naturally. This is one of the most practical and actionable verses in Proverbs: if you want peace, stop the flow of negative talk. Communities, families, and friendships that refuse gossip find their conflicts diminishing.
verses.prayer: God, help me never spread gossip.
verses.discussion_question: How does gossip keep arguments going longer?
verses.family_discussion: How do we create a family culture that actively starves gossip — where problems are addressed directly with the person involved rather than broadcast to others?
verses.do_it_today: If you hear gossip today, do not pass it on. Let it stop with you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A fire slowly dying out as no more wood is added, peaceful scene with smoke fading, a child watching the peace return, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
verses.little_bible: Hot coals make a fire hotter. More wood makes a fire bigger. A quarrelsome person makes every fight worse.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A quarrelsome person makes every argument grow bigger, just like wood feeds a fire.
verses.meaning: Some people are fire-starters by nature — they cannot resist adding fuel to conflict. The contentious person does not stumble into strife accidentally; they bring the coals and the wood that make it blaze. This is a sin of disposition: cultivating a heart that loves conflict is incompatible with wisdom.
verses.memory_phrase: Do not add fuel to fights.
verses.prayer: God, make me a peacemaker, not a fire-starter.
verses.discussion_question: What does it look like to make a fight bigger instead of smaller?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children recognise when they are feeding a conflict — through their words, their tone, or their choices — and call them to be active peacemakers instead?
verses.do_it_today: In any disagreement today, try to say one thing that calms things down rather than heats things up.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child adding logs to a fire that is already large, another child watching worriedly, the fire growing, warm cautionary watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
verses.little_bible: Gossip hurts like a deep wound. The pain goes all the way inside. It does not quickly go away.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Gossip cuts deep and hurts inside, like a wound.
verses.meaning: Gossip does not merely cause surface embarrassment — it wounds at depth. The image of words going into the 'innermost parts' pictures how gossip lodges in a person's heart, memory, and identity, doing damage long after the words are spoken. Words are not neutral; they have the power to wound and even to destroy.
verses.prayer: God, guard my mouth from words that wound.
verses.discussion_question: Why does hearing gossip about yourself hurt so deeply?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that words leave marks that linger — and that the words they choose today may stay with someone else for years?
verses.do_it_today: Choose one person today and say something genuinely kind and true to them. Heal with your words.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with a sad, wounded expression, hands over heart, while another child speaks nearby, deep hurt visible, warm gentle watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.
verses.little_bible: Smooth and flattering words that hide a wicked heart are like a broken pot covered in cheap silver. It looks fine. It is worthless inside.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Nice words from a wicked heart are worthless, like a broken pot covered in fake silver.
verses.meaning: A potsherd — a broken piece of pottery — covered with silver dross (the waste product of refining silver) looks impressive but is actually worthless. This is the picture of flattery: words that sound warm and fine but come from a wicked heart. The appearance of goodness is not the same as goodness.
verses.prayer: God, make my words and heart both clean.
verses.discussion_question: Why are nice words worthless if they do not come from an honest heart?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children understand the difference between genuine kindness and flattery — and develop the discernment to notice when someone's smooth words might be hiding something else?
verses.do_it_today: Make sure every kind thing you say today you really mean. Do not say kind things you do not mean.
verses.illustration_prompt: A broken clay pot painted with shiny silver on the outside but clearly cracked and hollow inside, a child examining it with surprise, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
verses.little_bible: Someone who hates you can smile and say nice things. But inside they are hiding deceit and ill-will.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A person who hates can smile on the outside while hiding evil inside.
verses.meaning: Dissembling means disguising one's true feelings and intentions. The person who hates uses their lips as a mask — speaking pleasantly while storing up deceit in their heart. This is the sin of hypocrisy at its most dangerous: hatred hidden behind a friendly face.
verses.prayer: God, help me be honest always, inside and out.
verses.discussion_question: How can someone hide hatred behind nice words?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop godly discernment about people — not cynicism, but a wise awareness that outward words do not always match inward intentions?
verses.do_it_today: Check your own heart today. Is there anyone you are being nice to on the outside but feeling angry about inside? Bring it to God.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with a broad smile on their face but a dark shadow across their heart, two faces — one visible, one hidden — gentle warning watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.
verses.little_bible: When this kind of person speaks kindly, do not trust it. Their heart is full of wicked and terrible things.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Smooth words can hide a heart full of terrible things. Be wise.
verses.meaning: 'Seven abominations' is a way of saying the wickedness in this person's heart is complete and manifold. The warning is clear: do not be disarmed by pleasant speech alone. Discernment means looking past the presentation to the pattern of a person's life and character.
verses.prayer: God, give me wisdom to see what is true.
verses.discussion_question: How do you know if you can really trust someone?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach children to make trustworthiness assessments wisely — not by paranoia, but by watching patterns of honesty, consistency, and character over time?
verses.do_it_today: Think about what makes someone truly trustworthy. List three things. Share them with a parent.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child listening to another child with very sweet words while wise parents in the background are watching carefully with concern, warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation.
verses.little_bible: Hidden hatred covered by lies will not stay hidden. One day God will bring all of it into the open. Everyone will see.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Hidden wickedness will one day be shown to everyone.
verses.meaning: No matter how cleverly wickedness is concealed — with smooth talk, pleasant manners, and deceitful cover — God ensures that it will be exposed. The 'whole congregation' pictures the community as the audience for God's justice. Secret sin is never permanent; exposure is God's sovereign guarantee.
verses.prayer: God, let me live with nothing to hide.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it always better to be honest than to hide what is wrong?
verses.family_discussion: How do we create a family culture where our children feel safe to confess and bring things into the light — so that the practice of hiding sin does not become deeply rooted in them?
verses.do_it_today: Is there anything you have been hiding from your parents? Today is a good day to tell the truth.
verses.illustration_prompt: A dark cloth being pulled back to reveal something hidden underneath, bright light flooding in, a figure looking caught but also relieved, warm watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
verses.little_bible: If you dig a pit to trap someone, you will fall into it yourself. If you roll a stone to crush someone, it will roll back and crush you.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: If you try to trap others, the trap will catch you instead.
verses.meaning: This is one of the Bible's clearest statements of the principle of reaping what you sow. Those who scheme to bring others down find their schemes rebounding upon themselves. Evil devised against others is not morally neutral — it carries a returning force. God's moral order ensures that wickedness eventually turns on its author.
verses.prayer: God, keep me from ever planning harm for others.
verses.discussion_question: What happens to people who set traps for others?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children that revenge, scheming, and trying to trap or embarrass others always costs them more than they gain — and that God's justice is far more reliable than our own attempts to 'get even'?
verses.do_it_today: If you have been plotting to get back at someone, give it to God today. Trust Him to be the judge.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child who has dug a hole to trap someone else, but accidentally steps backward into it themselves, surprised expression, gentle comic warning in warm watercolour

verses.kjv: A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin.
verses.little_bible: Lying shows hatred for the person you lie about. Flattery causes ruin. Both are forms of harm.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Lying and flattery both hurt and destroy people.
verses.meaning: The chapter closes with a devastating summary: lies are not merely errors — they are expressions of hatred toward the people they hurt. And flattery, which appears kind, actually works ruin. Both forms of dishonest speech — outright lies and smooth flattery — are at root acts of destruction. The antidote is a heart that loves truth and genuinely loves neighbour.
verses.prayer: God, fill my mouth with truth and love.
verses.discussion_question: Why are both lies and flattery harmful to people?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that truthful love — even when it involves saying hard things — is more genuinely kind than dishonest flattery that makes people feel good in the moment but leads them to harm?
verses.do_it_today: Say something true and kind to someone you love today. Make sure it is both — true and kind.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two paths diverging — one labelled with lies and flattery leading to a dark fallen city, one labelled with truth and love leading to a bright safe home, a child at the crossroads, warm watercolour illustration
